The Wood duck (Aix sponsa) is a cavity-nesting waterfowl species whose reproductive strategy reflects a balance between relatively high fecundity and substantial parental investment. Eggs are deposited in clutches ranging from 6 to 15 eggs [N_R_i = clutches ranging from 6 to 15 eggs], and females may produce one or two clutches per year [F_R_i = one or two clutches per year], which represents a substantial annual reproductive output for a duck of this body size. When incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the eggs hatch after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], although the documented range extends from 28 to 37 days depending on microclimatic conditions within the nest cavity. The newly hatched ducklings emerge at a wet weight of roughly 23.7 grams [Wwb = roughly 23.7 grams], a precocial mass that allows them to leave the nest within 24 hours. This initial body mass, known as the initial wet weight, is approximately 44 grams [Ww0 = approximately 44 grams] in the freshly laid egg, meaning the developing embryo acquires a significant portion of its hatching mass through the conversion of yolk and albumen reserves prior to hatching.

Under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of this species' active metabolic phase, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at approximately 61.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 61.5 days after hatching], although field ornithologists report a broader span of 56 to 70 days that reflects variability in local food abundance and brood size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively protracted fledging period is typical of cavity-nesting anatids, which benefit from reduced predation risk within the safe confines of the nest hole. The young are fed by both parents throughout this developmental phase, and the nestling chicks grow rapidly, accumulating body mass and maturing their flight feathers. The extended dependence period, compared to some ground-nesting ducks, is thought to enhance post-fledging survival.

The basal metabolic rate of this species, measured under standard respirometry conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reaches a maximum of 404.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 404.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic value is consistent with the energetic demands of a duck of this size and reflects the costs associated with maintaining a relatively high body temperature in an aquatic foraging environment. The resting oxygen consumption of the Wood duck is notably intermediate among North American waterfowl, falling below that of the smaller Green-winged Teal but exceeding that of the larger Mallard. Such differences in metabolic rate are partly attributable to variations in body mass, plumage insulation, and the energetic cost of thermoregulation in water. Researchers have noted that this metabolic rate is measured on post-absorptive, resting individuals during the inactive phase of their circadian cycle, ensuring that the value represents a true basal condition rather than activity-induced elevation.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a well-defined schedule under standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Puberty is attained at approximately 184.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 184.5 days after hatching], a relatively rapid progression that allows first-year birds to reach reproductive competence before the onset of the following breeding season at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This timing is crucial for a species that relies on the availability of suitable tree cavities for nesting, which may be scarce in some habitats. The first brood, however, is typically deferred until roughly 365 days after hatching [tR = roughly 365 days after hatching], meaning that most individuals do not successfully fledge their first brood until their second calendar year at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay between achieving physiological puberty and initiating actual reproduction reflects the time required for a young female to locate and compete for a suitable nest cavity, form a stable pair bond, and accumulate the necessary energy reserves for egg production.

Maximum documented lifespan for the Wood duck, recorded under field conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days], which corresponds to roughly 14 years of age. This longevity is notable for a species that experiences significant nest predation and hunting pressure. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 637 grams [Wwi = approximately 637 grams], while males reach a larger ultimate wet weight of about 680 grams [Wwi = about 680 grams], a modest but consistent sexual size dimorphism typical of many North American waterfowl. The heavier mass of the male is thought to confer advantages in defending territory and securing access to females during the breeding season. Comparative analyses show that this body mass is intermediate among cavity-nesting ducks, with the Wood duck being heavier than the smaller Hooded Merganser but considerably lighter than the much larger Common Goldeneye.
